newsitem.title: UK: UK's largest natural gas vehicle fleet launched.
newsitem.headline: UK's largest natural gas vehicle fleet launched.

text.p: Britain launched its largest fleet of natural gas vehicles and a filling station to serve them on Wednesday.

A fleet of 24 vehicles were produced by a partnership of gas utility Centrica plc, Fiat Ford joint venture Iveco Ford, Farid Municipal Vehicles, government agency the Energy Savings Trust and the southwest London Borough of Merton.
The fleet includes nine small vans, nine buses and six refuse trucks.
Centrica's British Gas Natural Gas Vehicles (NGV) installed the filling station for free. It will be available to other users, both private and commercial, as well as to Merton's own vehicles.
"Natural gas is now ready for road use," said Peter
Lehmann, commercial director of Centrica.
Gas vehicles were cleaner to run, produced less noxious emissions, and were quieter, he added.
Also speaking at the launch, environment minister Michael Meacher said the last government had published a strategy for air quality, and the new Labour regime would take this even further.

The most challenging objectives in the programme involved reducing levels of nitrogen dioxide and particulates, he said, adding that natural gas vehicles produce less of these emissions than conventional vehicles.
But while the benefits of natural gas are widely recognised, the obstacles for fleet users wishing to switch to this fuel remain formidable.
Meacher said there are two main barriers, the high cost of vehicles and the lack of infrastructure for refuelling.

He said the last government had reduced excise duties on road fuel gases, and chancellor Gordon Brown in his July budget had now frozen duties while raising them on gasoline and diesel, so widening the differential between fuels.
"He has made a commitment at least to maintain this differential, so prospective purchasers can be confident of lower bills at least for the life of this parliament," he said.
He added that natural gas vehicles attracted lower vehicle excise duty, and said these two factors "will go a long way to mitigate the capital cost."
The second barrier, the lack of infrastructure was described by Meacher as a "classic chicken and egg problem," with someone needed to take the initiative and install refuelling facilities.
Tom Gorman, general manager of British Gas NGV, said he would like to see a further reduction in excise duties.

He pointed out that they are now 21 pence a kilogramme, out of a BG sale price of 62.3 p/kg. He would like to see the duty fall to around 10 p/kg, pointing out that there are so few vehicles on the road using fuel gases that such a move "would cost nothing."

Fred Parker, executive director of the Natural Gas Vehicle Association (NGVA) said the European Union had established a recommended minimum level of duty on NGV's which member states must apply -- much lower than the equivalent level for gasoline and diesel.
Even so, he said, excise duties in Britain on gasoline and diesel are some 70 percent above the EU minimum level, while for natural gas it is 240 percent over the minimum.
The NGVA is campaigning to get the government to set the duty at the EU minimum level for a "sustainable period" of around five years to help boost the industry in Britain.
If the minimum duty applied, Parker said, the differential between the price of gasoline and natural gas at the pump would be around 35 pence a litre equivalent.
Meacher told the launch that Prime Minister Tony Blair is in the process of having his family Ford Galaxy converted to run on Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG).
--Sebastian Alison, London Newsroom, +44 171 542 6412
